questions.prompt: Why are the animations less useful for runners and cyclists?

options.label: B

questions.prompt: What other issue can change how a road signal is understood?

tests.title: Advanced: Connect design choices to road behaviour

groups.heading: Advanced: Connect design choices to road behaviour
groups.instruction: Listen to the episode and choose the best answer to each question. Questions follow the recording.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE answer: A, B or C.

questions.prompt: What communication problem does Professor Brewster identify?

options.label: A
options.text: A passenger must always give pedestrians spoken instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: Eye contact is only useful when everybody remains inside a vehicle.

options.label: C
options.text: Without a visible human driver, other users cannot negotiate priority in the usual way.

questions.prompt: What does Pippa suggest may change as people become familiar with autonomous vehicles?

options.label: A
options.text: They may become more accustomed to deciding how to interact with them.

options.label: B
options.text: Every possible danger will automatically disappear.

options.label: C
options.text: Road users will no longer need to judge when to cross.

questions.prompt: What lesson follows from the different results for pedestrians and faster road users?

options.label: A
options.text: A signal must suit the amount of viewing and decision time available.

options.label: B
options.text: One moving display is equally effective for every road user.

options.label: C
options.text: Faster movement gives a person more time to study an animation.

questions.prompt: Why are fixed coloured rings a useful alternative in the example?

options.label: A
options.text: They require viewers to watch a long sequence of changing images.

options.label: B
options.text: They depend on speaking the same language as a human driver.

options.label: C
options.text: They provide a signal that can be recognised in a brief look.

questions.prompt: What does the hand-waving example illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Every culture uses exactly the same road gestures.

options.label: B
options.text: A familiar gesture may convey different messages across cultures.

options.label: C
options.text: Waving has no communicative purpose in any culture.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison involving South Korea add to the discussion?

options.label: A
options.text: Robotic vehicles make local road rules irrelevant.

options.label: B
options.text: Safety also depends on local human behaviour, not just vehicle technology.

options.label: C
options.text: A country's culture determines the colour of every vehicle.
